text: More than 3,000 years ago, farmers made their homes at Ban Chiang, a village in northeast Thailand.
They grew rice, and one old pot found in a grave still held rice.
src: Ban Chiang is an archaeological site in Nong Han district, Udon Thani province, northeast Thailand / Charles Higham’s Bayesian analysis of human and animal bones instead put first settlement around 1500 BCE
Rice was grown / one in the lowest grave contained rice

text: They kept water buffalo and cattle, and they hunted wild cattle too.
Working closely with buffalo in the wet rice fields brought people new illnesses.
src: the water buffalo was a domesticated breed. Domestic cattle (B. taurus) were also common / Bones of two wild cattle, the gaur and B. javanicus, together with heavy butchery marks, point to hunting
The use of water buffalo in wet rice fields during the Early period (2100–900 BCE) is linked with new diseases caught through close contact with domesticated animals

text: The villagers made their own bronze, a metal made with copper, right in their village.
They cast bangles, rings, axes, hooks and small bells, but very few weapons.
src: most copper-alloy objects were cast in local villages, not in large central workshops / the villagers made their own metal objects from an early stage
Bronze finds include bracelets, rings, anklets, wires and rods, spearheads, axes and adzes, hooks, blades and small bells / the scarcity of metal weapons

text: In 1966 a student tripped over a tree root and fell onto the tops of buried pots.
Today Ban Chiang is a World Heritage Site, and its museum shows red-painted pots and graves as they were found.
src: Steve Young, a Harvard College student who spoke Thai and was living in the village to research his thesis, tripped over the root of a red kapok tree and fell onto the exposed tops of buried jars
Ban Chiang was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992 / The Ban Chiang National Museum presents the site / showing artefacts and replica skeletons as they were found / The red-painted pottery
